name: New York
tagline: Eight million stories, one relentless skyline and a slice at 2 a.m.
description:
New York moves at a pace that rewires you within an hour of landing. Steam curls from manholes, cabs lean on their horns, and a single block can hold a bakery, a gallery, a century-old tavern and somebody rehearsing for a Broadway audition. The skyline you have seen in a thousand films turns out to be even more improbable in person, especially from a ferry deck at dusk.

The city rewards travelers who walk. Tick off the headline sights, from the Statue of Liberty to the Met and the open-air deck of the Empire State Building, then let the neighborhoods do the rest: espresso and bookshops in the West Village, dumpling counters and dive bars on the Lower East Side, murals and rooftop bars across the river in Williamsburg. Central Park alone can absorb an entire unhurried day.

Food is the real common language. You can fold a two-dollar slice on the sidewalk after midnight, queue for hand-carved pastrami at lunch and splurge on a tasting menu that sets trends for kitchens worldwide, all within a few subway stops. Budget generously, because hotels here are among the priciest anywhere, but remember that some of the best shows, from buskers in Washington Square to the view from the Staten Island Ferry, cost nothing at all.

safety.notes: Tourist areas are busy, well-policed and generally safe day and night, but pickpockets work crowded spots like Times Square and packed subway cars. Late at night, ride in a carriage with other passengers and keep your phone out of reach near train doors.

tipping: Tip 18–22% at sit-down restaurants, $1–2 per drink at bars and 15–20% for taxis and rideshares; remember that 8.875% sales tax is added at the register on top of listed prices.
gettingAround: The 24-hour subway and bus network reaches almost everywhere; just tap a contactless card or phone at the turnstile using OMNY. In Midtown, walking is often faster than a cab, and Citi Bike docks cover Manhattan and much of Brooklyn for short hops.
tips: Tap the same card or phone for every subway ride: once you hit 12 paid rides within seven days, OMNY caps your fare and the rest of the week is free.
The Staten Island Ferry is free, runs 24/7 and glides right past the Statue of Liberty; stand on the right-hand side of the boat on the way out for the best view.
Buy Statue of Liberty tickets only from the official ferry operator's website, and ignore the costumed sellers around Battery Park pushing overpriced 'harbor tours'.
For discounted Broadway seats, check the TKTS booth in Times Square or enter the digital rush and lottery draws the morning of the show.
Several big museums run free or pay-what-you-wish evenings each week; check their websites and arrive 30 minutes early, because lines form fast.
Walk the Brooklyn Bridge from Brooklyn toward Manhattan so the skyline stays in front of you, and go before 8 a.m. to have the promenade almost to yourself.
etiquette: Keep moving on sidewalks and step to the side before stopping to check a map or take a photo.
On the subway, let riders off before you board, don't block the doors, and keep bags off empty seats.
New Yorkers are brisk rather than rude; a quick, direct question usually gets a friendly, direct answer.
Tipping is part of workers' wages here, so leaving little or nothing is considered a real insult.

"Deadass, the line for that bakery is around the block."
"Grab me a coffee from the bodega on the corner."

The front steps of a brownstone

"We were on line for an hour at the Met."

neighborhoods.name: Greenwich Village
neighborhoods.blurb: Crooked, tree-lined streets, brownstones and basement jazz clubs orbit Washington Square Park, where chess hustlers, students and buskers keep the arch buzzing.

neighborhoods.name: Lower East Side
neighborhoods.blurb: The old tenement district is now a nightlife hub of cocktail dens, vintage shops and galleries, anchored by storied delis and dumpling counters.

neighborhoods.name: Williamsburg
neighborhoods.blurb: Brooklyn's creative engine room, with rooftop bars, weekend flea markets, indie music venues and sweeping Manhattan views from its waterfront parks.

neighborhoods.name: Harlem
neighborhoods.blurb: Grand brownstone boulevards, Sunday gospel services, soul-food institutions and the legendary Apollo Theater keep Black music and culture front and center.

neighborhoods.name: DUMBO
neighborhoods.blurb: Cobblestones and converted warehouses squeezed between two bridges, with galleries, a waterfront park and the city's most photographed street view.

dishes.name: New York-style pizza
dishes.description: Wide, thin slices with a crisp-chewy crust, sold by the slice from counters citywide; fold it lengthwise and eat it on the move.

dishes.name: Bagel with lox and schmear
dishes.description: A dense, chewy bagel, boiled then baked, loaded with cream cheese, silky cured salmon, capers and red onion: the definitive weekend breakfast.

dishes.name: Pastrami on rye
dishes.description: Brined, spiced and smoked beef brisket, steamed until tender and piled high on seeded rye with sharp brown mustard.

dishes.name: New York cheesecake
dishes.description: Taller, denser and richer than most, built on cream cheese and a graham-cracker crust, and best eaten plain.

dishes.name: Chopped cheese
dishes.description: A bodega-grill classic of ground beef, onions and melted American cheese chopped together on the flat-top and stuffed into a hero roll.

events.name: Tribeca Festival
events.description: Launched to revive Lower Manhattan after 2001, it fills downtown with film premieres, free outdoor screenings and talks with directors and stars.

events.name: Village Halloween Parade
events.description: Tens of thousands of costumed revelers, giant puppets and marching bands take over Sixth Avenue on Halloween night, and anyone in costume can join in.

events.name: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
events.description: Towering character balloons drift down Central Park West on Thanksgiving morning; watch them being inflated near the Natural History Museum the evening before.

events.name: New Year's Eve in Times Square
events.description: Around a million people pack Midtown to watch the crystal ball drop at midnight; arrive by mid-afternoon and expect no bathroom access once you're in the pens.

attractions.name: Central Park
attractions.description: More than 800 acres of meadows, rocky outcrops and lakes carved out of the middle of Manhattan, where joggers, jazz trios and softball leagues share the lawns. Wander from the tiled arcade of Bethesda Terrace to the birding trails of the Ramble, then sprawl on Sheep Meadow with the skyline rising over the trees.
attractions.bookingTip: No ticket needed, but rent a rowboat at the Loeb Boathouse before noon on summer weekends to dodge the long wait.

attractions.name: Statue of Liberty
attractions.description: Lady Liberty's copper robe has weathered to its famous sea-green over 140 years, and watching her grow larger from the ferry rail never gets old. Pair the island with the immigration museum on neighboring Ellis Island, where you can search historic passenger lists for your own ancestors.
attractions.hours: Ferries roughly 09:00–15:30 daily from Battery Park
attractions.bookingTip: Book on the official ferry website and reserve crown access months ahead; pedestal slots also sell out in summer.

attractions.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
attractions.description: Five thousand years of human creativity fill this Fifth Avenue colossus, from a complete Egyptian temple bathed in afternoon light to Vermeers, Van Goghs and armored knights on horseback. Nobody sees it all, so pick three galleries, then finish at the seasonal rooftop garden for a drink above the park's canopy.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy timed tickets online to skip the line on the front steps, and head to the Temple of Dendur first before tour groups arrive.

attractions.name: Brooklyn Bridge
attractions.description: Its granite Gothic towers and web of steel cables made it the world's longest suspension bridge in 1883, and the raised wooden promenade is still the city's most cinematic stroll. Cross at sunrise for soft light and near-empty planks, then drop into DUMBO for coffee and the famous framed view down Washington Street.
attractions.bookingTip: Take the subway to High Street in Brooklyn and walk toward Manhattan so the skyline is ahead of you the entire way.

attractions.name: High Line
attractions.description: A disused freight railway reborn as a ribbon of wild grasses, sculpture and sun loungers floating three stories above the West Side. Along the way you look straight down avenues, into gallery windows and past buildings by some of the world's boldest architects.
attractions.bookingTip: Enter at Gansevoort Street about an hour before sunset and walk north as the light turns gold over the Hudson.

attractions.name: Empire State Building
attractions.description: The Art Deco spire that defined the word skyscraper still delivers the classic view from its open-air 86th-floor deck, where wind whips through the railings and Midtown's grid runs to every horizon. Late-night visits, when crowds thin and the city glitters, are often the best of all.
attractions.bookingTip: Book a timed ticket for the hour before sunset to see the city in daylight, at dusk and lit up in one visit.

attractions.name: Times Square
attractions.description: A canyon of giant LED screens that turns night into a strange electric noon, packed with costumed characters, street performers and wide-eyed visitors. Locals avoid it, but seeing it blazing once is a rite of passage: climb the red glass steps for the full panorama, then slip into a Broadway theater a block away.
attractions.bookingTip: The TKTS booth under the red steps sells same-day discounted Broadway seats; queue before it opens for the widest choice.

attractions.name: National September 11 Memorial & Museum
attractions.description: Two vast square pools sit in the footprints of the Twin Towers, their waterfalls vanishing into a central void while nearly 3,000 names are cut into the bronze parapets. Beneath the plaza, the museum retells the day through twisted steel, recovered belongings and recorded voices; it is profoundly moving and best visited early.
attractions.bookingTip: The outdoor memorial pools are free; book museum tickets online and allow at least two unhurried hours for the emotionally heavy galleries.

attractions.name: Museum of Modern Art
attractions.description: Van Gogh's swirling night sky, Monet's water lilies, Warhol's soup cans and Frida Kahlo's self-portraits are only the start at the world's defining collection of modern art. The sculpture garden, with its birch trees and Rodin bronzes, is one of Midtown's calmest corners.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy timed entry online and ride straight to the fifth floor at opening; The Starry Night draws a crowd by mid-morning.

attractions.name: Chelsea Market
attractions.description: The old biscuit factory where the Oreo was invented is now a brick-and-iron food hall crammed with taco counters, lobster rolls, bakeries and spice merchants. It's the easiest one-stop graze in Manhattan and the perfect refuel before or after the High Line.
attractions.bookingTip: Come on a weekday before noon to graze without elbowing through weekend crowds, then climb the stairs to the High Line next door.

hotels.name: The Aldermoor on Fifth
hotels.description: A limestone Gilded Age mansion turned hotel a few steps from the park, where afternoon tea is poured beneath a coffered ceiling and suites come with butler service and marble soaking tubs. Upper-floor park-view rooms look straight across the treetops to the Ramble.

hotels.name: Cobblestone & Crane
hotels.description: A converted 19th-century coffee warehouse on a cobbled DUMBO lane, with timber beams, arched windows and a rooftop bar that frames the Brooklyn Bridge like a postcard. Rooms pair Brooklyn-made furniture with deep tubs and turntables stocked with local vinyl.

hotels.name: Ninth Avenue Bunkhouse
hotels.description: A cheerful walk-up hostel with curtained pod bunks, a communal kitchen and nightly events from pizza crawls to Broadway lottery parties. It's the cheapest decent bed within walking distance of the theaters.

hotels.name: The Tinsmith Lofts
hotels.description: Floor-to-ceiling glass, polished concrete and gallery-grade art define this angular tower that seems to lean over the High Line. Corner rooms have freestanding tubs facing the Hudson, and the lobby bar becomes a DJ-fueled scene on weekends.

hotels.name: The Maiden Lane Exchange
hotels.description: A 1920s bank headquarters where the gilded banking hall now pours cocktails and the old vault holds a wine cellar. Rooms are generous by Manhattan standards, and weekend rates drop sharply once the Wall Street crowd heads home.

hotels.name: Madison Keyhouse Suites
hotels.description: Studios and one-bedroom apartments with full kitchens inside a converted garment-trade loft building, ideal for families or longer stays. Many north-facing windows catch the Empire State Building's nightly light show.

restaurants.name: Gansevoort Bagel Bakery
restaurants.description: Kettle-boiled, hand-rolled bagels leave the deck oven every half hour, glossy and blistered, beside a counter of whitefish salad, scallion schmear and translucent Nova lox. Expect a line of construction crews and gallery assistants by 8 a.m.; it moves fast.
restaurants.signatureDish: Everything bagel with scallion cream cheese and Nova lox

restaurants.name: Slice of the Deuce
restaurants.cuisine: New York pizza by the slice
restaurants.description: A narrow, fluorescent-lit counter that feeds post-show crowds until 4 a.m. with thin, foldable, char-blistered slices. The plain cheese slice is the benchmark; add a crisp Sicilian square if you're sharing.

restaurants.name: Fulton Ferry Oyster Room
restaurants.description: A white-tiled raw bar tucked under the bridge approach, shucking a dozen East Coast oyster varieties with chalkboard notes on salinity and finish. Grab a window seat when the East River turns copper at sunset and order the lobster roll.
restaurants.signatureDish: Warm lobster roll with brown butter

restaurants.name: Aurelian & Rye
restaurants.description: A hushed, walnut-paneled dining room where ten courses trace the Hudson Valley through the seasons: Long Island duck, Catskills trout, cider caramel. The wine list leans into Finger Lakes Rieslings, and the eight-seat chef's counter books out a month ahead.
restaurants.signatureDish: Dry-aged Long Island duck with Concord grape jus

restaurants.name: Charcoal Lantern K-Town
restaurants.description: Up a narrow staircase on 32nd Street, tables glow over live-charcoal grills while servers snip sizzling short rib with scissors and keep the banchan coming. It stays loud and busy until the small hours, which makes it perfect after a night on the observation deck.
restaurants.signatureDish: Galbi (marinated beef short rib) with lettuce wraps

restaurants.name: Yorkville Rye House
restaurants.description: The pastrami is brined for ten days, smoked overnight and hand-carved into sandwiches so tall you'll need a knife and fork. Wisecracking waiters, bowls of sour pickles on every table and a chocolate egg cream make it the ideal post-museum refuel.
restaurants.signatureDish: Hand-carved pastrami on rye with deli mustard

restaurants.name: Amsterdam Avenue Griddle & Bake
restaurants.description: A sunny corner café that bakes its own sourdough and turns out fluffy buttermilk pancakes, shakshuka and serious flat whites for stroller-pushing locals. Grab a pastry to go and you're two blocks from the park's western entrance.
restaurants.signatureDish: Buttermilk pancakes with Vermont maple syrup

restaurants.name: Pearl & Broad Chophouse
restaurants.description: Leather banquettes, white-jacketed waiters and a glass-walled dry-aging room set the scene for a proper Wall Street steak dinner. Share the porterhouse with creamed spinach and hash browns, and save room for cheesecake.
restaurants.signatureDish: Dry-aged porterhouse for two with creamed spinach

experiences.name: Harbor Lights Schooner Sail
experiences.description: Glide past Lady Liberty and the Lower Manhattan skyline aboard a restored wooden schooner as the sun sinks behind New Jersey and the towers light up. The crew hoists the sails by hand, and guests are welcome to take a turn on the lines.

experiences.name: Bridge & Brooklyn Bites Walk
experiences.description: Cross the Brooklyn Bridge with a local food writer, then graze through DUMBO and Brooklyn Heights on coal-oven pizza, smoked fish, Caribbean patties and a scoop of small-batch ice cream. Along the way you'll hear how waves of immigrants shaped what New Yorkers eat.

experiences.name: Village Jazz Cellar Crawl
experiences.description: Meet at the southern end of the High Line, then descend into three of Greenwich Village's basement jazz rooms with a musician-guide who knows the house bands and saves you seats. Between sets, hear stories of the Beat poets and folk singers who made these streets famous.

experiences.name: Hand-Rolled Bagel Workshop
experiences.description: Learn why New York bagels taste different in a hands-on class with a third-generation baker: shape, cold-proof, kettle-boil in malted water and bake your own dozen. You'll leave with the dough recipe, a tub of homemade schmear and a new respect for your morning bagel.
includes: A dozen bagels to take home
